en: Homage to the Blessed Noble Mahāpratisarā, the Queen of Vidyās! Homage to the Truly Enlightened Ones!
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the gabled pavilion on the peak of Vajrameru,
established upon the ground of the Great Vajra Samādhi, adorned with the great vajra wish-fulfilling trees,
and illuminated by the radiance of precious lotuses in the great vajra ponds.
On ground prepared with great vajra-sand,
in a place empowered by the great vajra,
within the great vajra-maṇḍala pavilion.
In the palace of Śakra, the lord of the gods,
which was resplendent with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great vajra lion-thrones,
and endowed with the miracle of eloquence in teaching the Dharma.
It was empowered by the empowerment of all Buddhas, entered into the equality of all phenomena, and led to omniscience;
together with eighty-four hundred thousand *koṭī-niyuta* of Bodhisattvas,

all of whom were bound to one more birth (*ekajāti*), irreversible from unexcelled perfect enlightenment, possessed of great power, and capable of displaying the great miracles of the transformations of Buddha-fields through the *mahāvajra-vimokṣa-samādhi*.

They manifested the miracle of eloquence in teaching the Dharma—vivid, sweet, noble, and profound—which enters into the mental conduct of all sentient beings in a single moment, a single thought-instant, or a single muhūrta;

they were possessed of the mastery of incalculable clouds of great offerings to the Tathāgatas in many buddha-fields, as well as the doors of liberation, dhāraṇīs, samādhis, sovereign powers, superknowledges, the unique qualities of a Buddha, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the stages, the perfections, skill in means, the means of integration, and the great love, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; their mental continuums were secluded, purified, and stainless, such as [the one] with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha.
And by Vajranetra,
and by Vajragātra,
and by Vajramati.
And by Vajrahasta,
and by Vajrasaṃhata,
and by Vajranārāyaṇa.
And Vajravikurvin,
and Vajrakūṭa,
and Vajrarāśi.
And with Vajrāṅkuśa,
and with Suvajra,
and with Vajrasena.
and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Vajraketu;

Thus, together with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas led by these foremost ones, and with a great multitude of great śrāvakas— all of whom were arhats, whose outflows were exhausted, who had severed the fetters of existence, whose minds were perfectly liberated through right knowledge, whose wisdom was well-liberated, who had attained the great power of the miraculous transformations of the inconceivable strength of samādhi, who possessed unimpeded vision of knowledge, and who were all free from stain, having burned away the seeds of the habitual tendencies of affliction— [the Blessed One resided].
Namely, with the venerable Śāradvatīputra, the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
and the venerable Kaphina.
And with the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Revata, and the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
And with the venerable Cunda,
the venerable Nanda,
and the venerable Sunanda.
And with the Venerable Kāśyapa,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa,
and the Venerable Nandīkāśyapa.
By the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa and by the Venerable Gayākāśyapa.

Thus, together with a great multitude of principal great śrāvakas, and with incalculable, immeasurable, and ineffably ineffable sons of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm, headed by the son of the gods Maheśvara.
And with Brahmā Sahāpati,
with the sons of the gods headed by the Brahmakāyika devaputras,
and with the devaputra Suyāma.
Together with the retinue of the sons of the gods belonging to the Suyāma host,
the retinue of the son of the gods Saṃtuṣita,
and [the retinue] of Nirmāṇarati.
And by Paranirmitavaśavartin,
and by Śakra,
the lord of the gods, together with his retinue of all the sons of the gods.
And by Vemacitrin, the lord of the asuras, and by Bali and Prahlāda.
And by Rāhu, and by Vairocana, and by Subāhu.
Thus, with these as their leaders, there were immeasurable, incalculable, and innumerable lords of the asuras.
And by the naga king Sāgara,
and by Takṣaka,
and by Vāsuki.
And by Śaṅkhapāla, and by Karkoṭaka, and by Padma.
And with Mahāpadma;
thus led by these, there were immeasurable, incalculable, and innumerable nāga kings.
And by Druma, the king of the kinnaras,
accompanied by a retinue of many kinnaras.
And with the Gandharva king Pañcaśikha,
accompanied by a retinue of many Gandharva kings.
And by the Vidyādhara king Sarvārthasiddha,
together with a retinue of many Vidyādhara kings.
And by Suparṇākṣa, the king of Garuḍas,
together with a retinue of many kings of Garuḍas.
And by Vaiśravaṇa,
and by Māṇibhadra,
and by Pūrṇabhadra.
And by Pañcika, the king of the yakṣas,
accompanied by a retinue of many yakṣa kings.
And by Hārītī with her retinue of five hundred sons;
by the seven Mothers of the World;
by the seven great rākṣasīs; and by the seven most excellent great ṛṣis.
And by those who move through the atmosphere, by all the lunar mansions, planets, and deities,
by the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions,
and by the Earth and Sarasvatī.
And by the bhūtas, the vighnas, and the vināyakas; by the pretas and those of great supernatural power (maharddhika); by all the kings of mountains;
and by Varuṇa, the world-protector (lokapāla).
Together with the retinue of all the ocean deities,
and with Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, Daṇḍapāṇi,
and Naiguta.
And with Jātavedas,
and with the seven great winds,
and with Īśāna together with his consort.
Accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of followers.
And by Nārāyaṇa with his retinue;
and by Dantaka, Dāmaka, Lohaka, and Mohaka;
and by Mahāgaṇapati.
And with Megholka,
and Vināyakendra,
accompanied by a retinue of many obstacles and *vināyakas*.
And with Koṭagiri, and with the four sisters together with their brother.
And with Vajrāṅkuśī,
and with Vajraśaṅkarī,
and with the sixty-four Vajrahūtīs.
And with Vajrasena and Subāhu,
and Mūrdhaṭaka,
together with a retinue of many vajra families.
And by others who were devoted to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;

and by immeasurable, incalculable, and innumerable gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, sādhyas, sāhillakas, and oṣṭrakas.
And by the divine son Sūrya,
and by the divine son Candra,
and by the divine son Sucandra.
And by the deity Sandhyā,
and by the deity Uṣas,
and by all those who go.
And with the deity Rodasī,
and together with the deity Prajāpati.
Moreover, the Blessed One had thus well set in motion the wheel of Dharma; his Buddha-activity was perfectly completed; his equipment of merit and wisdom was fully perfected;

he had attained the ground of the perfection of the great awakening of omniscience and was well embraced by it; his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, radiant and resplendent; he shone with the eighty minor characteristics; all his limbs and members were beautiful; and his crown was invincible, as no sentient being could look upon it.

He was skilled in all the activities of Māra; he possessed the five kinds of eyes of knowledge regarding all sentient beings; he was endowed with the excellence of all modes; he was possessed of the knowledge of the omniscient one;
he was endowed with all the qualities of a Buddha.
He was the crusher of all hosts of Māras, adversaries, and evil factions; his fame, renown, and verses of praise rose up high as he roared the lion’s roar of the bull.
With the darkness of ignorance completely severed,

his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, having been brought forth through the practice of difficult austerities and the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, wisdom, skillful means, power, and aspiration— each performed hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of times beyond measure or calculation;
he sat upon a lion throne within a great vajra-jewel lotus-womb.
It was firmly established upon footstools fashioned from many vajra-jewel railings;
it was adorned with fragrant incense-stands bound with strings of red pearls emerging from the mouths of many makaras made of vajra-jewels;
and it resounded with the tinkling of networks of many small bells made of vajra-jewels.

He was seated upon a vajra-jewel lotus throne as vast as Mount Sumeru, graced by many wish-fulfilling trees; it was all-purifying, illuminated by networks of light rays from karketana, mahākarketana, indranīla, and puṣparāga gems set in the centers of many vajra-jewels; and it was surrounded by the shade provided by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of uplifted parasols adorned with many vajra-jewel stalks.
Blazing with splendor like the king of golden mountains, his ground shone with a single radiant halo as if from a thousand suns;
like the full orb of the moon, he was pleasing to behold for all the world; and like a great kalpa-tree, he taught the Dharma, fully blossomed with the qualities of a Buddha.

He proclaimed the holy life (brahmacarya) that is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end, possessing good meaning and well-phrased, entirely complete, pure, and immaculate.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One emitted from the circle of hair between his eyebrows a network of light rays named "Manifestation of All Buddhas.
By that blaze of light rays, this trichiliocosm great thousandfold world system was illuminated and made manifest.
And as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, all of them were pervaded and illuminated by that radiance.

And those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who were teaching the Dharma in those Buddha-fields— residing in palatial mansions and gabled towers adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lion-thrones—
together with great śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, and together with gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
Then the Blessed One addressed that vast assembly.
Now, therefore, out of compassion for all sentient beings, I shall proclaim the Mahāpratisarā, the great vidyā-mantra—
a dhāraṇī that crushes all evil-doers and all malevolent forces,
by the mere hearing of which sins go to their destruction.
Bestowing happiness upon all sentient beings and liberating them from all diseases,
it was spoken out of compassion for all sentient beings by the Lord of the World.
Having performed this protection for the sake of safeguarding all embodied beings who have committed evil deeds, one may enter the abode of the Asuras.
Likewise, one should go to Aḍakavatī, the abode of yakṣas on earth,
during a battle that is terrifying and fierce with bhūtas, nāgas, and piśācas.
Invincible to all enemies and even to the hosts of all beings,
all malevolent spirits (grahas) perish through the mere chanting of their names.
Those possessed by the humors, madness, epilepsy, piśācas, and ḍākinī-grahas—
those who consume vital energy and possess great splendor— harass the human race.
They all become paralyzed by the splendor of the Pratisarā;
hostile armies are destroyed, as are those terrible spells of bewitchment (kākhordas).
Spells and rituals do not afflict him; he is liberated from root-rites (mūlakarma).
Neither poison, nor slow-acting poison (gara), nor fire, nor weapon, nor even water can harm him.
Neither thunderbolts nor lightning, nor the winds of time, can cause him harm;
for by the splendor of the King of Vidyās, he utterly crushes all enemies.
Obstacles perish, diseases do not even arise,
all his aims are accomplished, and he constantly attains victory.
Whoever constantly wears this vidyā around the neck or on the arm, all his undertakings will succeed; of this there is no doubt.
The lords of the gods always protect them, as do the kings of the nāgas,
the bodhisattvas of great heroism, the Buddhas, and the Pratyekabuddha leaders.
The disciples of all the Buddhas and the powerful goddesses of knowledge constantly provide protection for the wearer of the Pratisarā.
Vajrapāṇi, the lord of yakṣas, and likewise the four kings will provide protection for him day and night; of this there is no doubt.
And Śakra, together with the three classes of gods, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara,
Nandikeśa, Mahākāla, Kārttikeya, and Gaṇeśvara.
All the hosts of Mātṛs, as well as others belonging to the retinue of Māra,
and the sages of great splendor, and the gods of great supernatural power;
The Buddhas, the great-souled ones, and the powerful goddesses of knowledge will indeed constantly provide protection for the wearer of the *pratisarā*.
Possessing great heroism, great splendor, and great strength and prowess,
they are Māmakī, Bhṛkuṭī, the goddess Tārā, and likewise Aṅkuśī.
Vajrasaṃkalā, Śvetā, and likewise Mahāśvetā;
Mahākālī and the messengers (dūtīs), as well as other Vajra-messengers (vajradūtīs).
Supāśī, Vajrapāśī, Cakrapāṇi, and Mahābalā;
Vajramālā, the Great Vidyā, and likewise Amṛtakuṇḍali.
The great goddess Aparājitā, Kālakarṇī of great strength,
as well as Dhanyā of great fortune, and Padmakuṇḍalī too.
Puṣpadantī, Maṇicūḍā, Svarṇakeśī, Piṅgalā, Mahātejā, Mahādevī, Dhanyā, and Vidyunmālinī.
The Rākṣasī Ekajaṭā, the leader of the Buddha’s retinue,
the highly fortunate Kāpālinī, the auspicious one, and likewise Laṅkeśvarī.
And many other vidyās that bestow favor upon sentient beings will provide protection for him in whose hand this vidyā resides.
Hārītī and Pāñcika, Śaṅkhinī and Kūṭadantinī,
as well as the goddess Śrī and Sarasvatī, protect him always as their followers.
Whatever woman always wears this Mahāpratisarā,
she shall attain all accomplishments, and her womb shall perpetually bear sons.
The fetuses grow in comfort, the pregnant woman gives birth easily, and diseases as well as all evils perish; of this there is no doubt.
He will always be meritorious and powerful, his wealth and grain will increase,
his words will be authoritative, and he will become worthy of honor.
Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever, being pure, enters [this place],
shall become a lord of liberation for all sentient beings through the arising [of this practice].
And he shall always be happy, free from all diseases.
The kings, along with their harems and great retinues, were under his control.
He constantly blazes with splendor, his mass of merit increases,
and all ritual procedures (kalpas) are accomplished for him once he has entered all maṇḍalas.
Knowing the samaya everywhere according to the word of the Jina,
he is not afflicted by bad dreams, for he is devoted to the removal of all evils.
Sins are destroyed, as are adversaries;
this was spoken by the Great Lords of Knowledge for the purpose of destroying all malevolent grahas.
For this [mantra] grants all desires; whoever should cultivate it constantly, I shall now proclaim that—let the hosts of spirits listen to me!
Homage to the Buddha.
Homage to the Dharma. Homage to the Saṅgha.
Homage to all Tathāgatas; homage, repeated homage! Homage to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Dharma, and Saṅgha!

O Blessed One, wearer of the jewel crown and garland;
O Blessed One, wearer of many various and manifold garments;
O Blessed One, Great Vidyā Goddess, protect, protect! (Mp_8)
O Purifier of all sins on every side, protect me and my retinue, as well as all sentient beings!

Huru 2, muru 2, rakṣa 2! Deliver me and all sentient beings who are without a protector, without a refuge, and without a resort from all sufferings! O Fierce One, O Fierce One, O Fierce One, O Swift One, O Warder-off of all the wicked, O Bearer of Victory!
Huru 2, muru 2, curu 2, turu 2! O protector of life, subduer of the best of gods, you who are worshipped by all the hosts of deities!
Cili 2, dhili 2, O you who look upon all things!

O Radiance! O Excellent Radiance! O Pure One of Excellent Radiance! O Purifier of All Evils! Dhuru, dhuru! O Supporter of the Earth! Dharā, dharā! Sumu, sumu! Musu, musu! O You of Luminous Splendor! Shake all the wicked! Fulfill my hope, O Purifier of All Evils! O Śrīvasudharā! O Jayakamalā!

Pavitramukhi! Khaṅgini, khaṅgini! Khara, khara! O you whose crest is ablaze! O you whose radiance is beheld on all sides!
O you of excellent and pure radiance!
O you whose pure light is spread everywhere!
Blaze, blaze! You who attract all the gods!
Satyaprati! Oṃ hrī traṃ tara tara tāraya tāraya me and all sentient beings, O Nāgavilokite!
Lahu lahu hulu hulu hutu hutu turu turu kiṇi kiṇi kṣiṇi kṣiṇi huni huni, O devourer of all grahas!

Save us, O Blessed One, from these most terrible fears.
O you who are purified by the vajra-flames through the binding of the vajra-fence and vajra-noose everywhere and on all sides; O Blessed One, you who purify the womb, you who fill the belly!
Bhuri 2! Bhagavati! Garbhasaṃśodhani! Kukṣisaṃpūraṇi!
Blaze, blaze! Move, move! O Jvālānī! May the gods rain down divine water from all sides; O you who rain down nectar, O you who cause the descent of the deities!
May they consecrate me with the supreme nectar of the words of the excellent Sugatas, for the sake of a supreme body; protect me everywhere and at all times!

From all fears, from all calamities, from all portents, from all diseases, for those terrified by the fear of all malevolent beings, you are the purifier of all strife, quarrels, conflicts, disputes, bad dreams, evil omens, and inauspicious sins; you are the destroyer of all yakṣas, rākṣasas, and nāgas!
Move, move, O powerful one!

The Aparājitā Mahādhāraṇī, the Heart of the Great Seal of the Wish-Fulfilling Gem, which radiates the purity of a universal garland of flames— at that very time, a great brahmin had gathered and was seated in that same assembly.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Great Brahmā:

"Great Brahmā, by merely reciting the thousandfold description of this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Vidyās, that son of noble family or daughter of noble family shall be completely liberated from all evil.
Furthermore, for one in whose heart this [spell] resides,"
O Great Brahmin, he should be known as one with a vajra-body; fire shall not take hold of his body. Why is this so? Because it is designated as such.

I know this: when the prince Rāhulabhadra was in his mother’s womb in the great and excellent city of Kapilavastu, and when six years had passed since Prince Sarvārthasiddha had pressed his foot against my navel and emerged,
I knew that it was none other than he.
While they were being tormented by scattered fires, poisonous water, and heated axes, I then became Aparājitā.
Then Gopā, the Śākya maiden, threw herself into a pit of fire;
thereupon, a lotus pond appeared.
At that time, while still within his mother’s womb, the noble youth Rāhula brought this spell to mind;
by the mere recollection of this spell,
even he attained a state of coolness at that very moment.
Then the body of Gopā, the Śākya maiden, was not touched by fire.
For what reason? Because this knowledge is empowered by all the Tathāgatas;
for that reason, this great Brahmin fire does not burn her.
Nor can he be deprived of life by means of poison;
how so?

O Great Brāhmaṇa, when the son of the merchant-foreman Koṣavaṇij was a master of spells in the great and excellent city of Śūrpāraka, he used the power of those spells to summon Takṣaka, the king of the nāgas. Having summoned him, he bound him by force, yet because of his immense size, the serpent became uncontrollable until he bit him out of anger.
He experiences intense, harsh, and bitter pain,
such that he knows, "My life has ceased.
There, many disputants were summoned.
And no one was able to treat the poison.

Now, in that very same excellent great city of Śūrpāraka, there lived a laywoman named Vimalaviśuddhi. Endowed with great compassion, this Queen of Great Spells (mahāvidyārājñī) was present upon the tip of her tongue.
She approached him; having approached, she set forth this great vidyā-mantra.

As soon as it was recollected by her at that single moment, he was rendered free from poison, his memory restored, and having been liberated from that great calamity, she caused this very great vidyā-mantra to be held in the heart of Śuddhiputra.
"According to the rule as it has been authorized."
Furthermore, Great Brahmin, what was fully understood?
While wandering gradually through the great city of Vārāṇasī, he came to be known as King Brahmadatta.
A neighboring king with a wheel of power, having mobilized a fourfold army, surrounded the great city of Vārāṇasī and began to destroy it.
Then the ministers informed King Brahmadatta:
"Your Majesty, the city has been seized by a hostile army.
Therefore, what means indeed should we employ so that this hostile army may be destroyed?"
"Give your command.
The king said, "Be of little anxiety; do not be concerned."
I possess a queen of spells named Mahāpratisarā,
by means of which I shall defeat this fourfold army here;
I will act accordingly.
The ministers prostrated with their heads and said, "What is this, Great King? Has this never been heard by us before?
The king replied:
"I shall now provide a direct vision.
Then King Brahmadatta,
having bathed with various scented waters, with his head washed and wearing pure garments, [recited] this Mahāpratisarā, the Queen of Great Spells.
Having written it according to the prescribed rite and placed it upon the hair of his head, and having made this very Queen of Great Knowledge his armor,
he entered the midst of battle alone; yet that entire fourfold army was defeated by him and utterly crushed until they were at his feet.
Having done this, that king of the wheel of power was liberated.
Thus indeed, O Great Brahmin, this Queen of Great Spells of great majesty, empowered by the heart-seals of all the Tathāgatas, is directly manifest.
It should be held as being directly manifest;
she is to be regarded as equal to all the Tathāgatas.

O Great Brahmin, whoever in the future time, in the final age, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of those beings who are short-lived, unfortunate, lacking in merit, and of meager fortune, shall write down this Queen of Great Spells according to the ritual and wear it on their arm or neck,
should be known as empowered by all the Tathāgatas.
It should be known as the body of all Tathāgatas;
it should be known as the vajra-body;
it should be known as the womb containing the essence of all Tathāgatas.
He should be known as the Eye of all Tathāgatas;
he should be known as one whose body is ablaze with flames;
he should be known as one possessing an impenetrable armor.
He should be known as the crusher of all enemies;
he should be known as the burner away of all sinful obscurations;
he should be known as the purifier of all rebirths in the hells.

"O Great Brahmin, why was it previously known that in a certain region of the earth there was a monk who was faithless, a violator of the training of the Tathāgata’s family, a thief, and a stealer of the gates of happiness; one who, having taken whatever property belonged to the Saṅgha, to the monks of the four quarters, to the stūpas, or to the community, made it his own personal possession and, having appropriated it all, exhausted it?"
Then, at another time, he was afflicted by a great illness and experienced intense painful sensations;
that ascetic, without protection, without refuge, and without a resort, uttered a great cry of lamentation.
Now, in that very region of the earth, there lived a lay follower who was a brahmin.
He heard that sound, and having heard it, he approached the monk; having approached him, he had this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells, written down and tied it around the neck of that monk.
As soon as the Great Amulet, the Great Queen of Vidyās, had been bound [upon him], all the sensations of that monk were stilled;
he was completely freed from all diseases and became healthy. That very night, when his end had arrived, he regained mindfulness and passed away.
At that very moment, having been cast down, he was reborn in the great Avīci hell; meanwhile,
his dead body was placed upon a funeral pyre by the monks,
and that Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells, remained fastened around his neck.
Immediately upon his rebirth, all the painful sensations of those hell-beings in that great Avīci hell were stilled; those hell-beings became endowed with every happiness,
and even those great masses of fire in Avīci were completely extinguished in every respect.
Then those messengers of Yama, filled with amazement, reported this decision of Yama, the King of Dharma, in detail.
"O Lord, this is seen as a source of great wonder within the perils of hell:
the terrible sufferings born of the karma of sentient beings have been stilled;
even those embers situated upon the bodies of embodied beings have been extinguished."
The saw-blades do not cause harm, the razor-edges do not catch,
the iron śālmalī trees are shattered, and the iron cauldrons have been stilled.
In the forest of sword-leaves, the leaves do not cause pain, for that is born of karma;
you are Yama, the King of Dharma, and you govern the people according to dharma.
"You ought to tell us this reason, for it is no small matter.
Then that King of Dharma, whose soul was righteousness and who was firm in his resolve regarding dharma, spoke.
Having heard such words from those who had perished on the bed of compassion, he spoke these words: "What is this? Tell me quickly; how did it happen?"
Then those extremely fierce servants of Yama heard these words from Yama, the King of Dharma, concerning those wicked beings:
"O King, this Great Being has arisen in the peril of hell;
because its name is Avīci, it is called the peril of hell."
Indeed, it is by the diversity of one's karma that beings are made happy;
for those who are happy everywhere indeed go again to the abode of the gods.
Even Yama, the King of Dharma, seeing this, spoke in amazement:
"He possesses great supernatural power, and his body from a previous birth is truly vast."
Just as a stupa is eternally beautified by a multitude of hundreds of jewels,
so too does his body shine when the *pratisarā* is bound around his neck.
Then those *yakṣa* guardians of hell spoke these words to Yama, the King of Dharma:
"O Lord, why is this called 'Pratisarā'?
The King of Dharma replied:
Whoever causes one to remember the practice does not go to an evil destiny; rather, being cultivated through the Pratisarā, he goes to a happy destiny.
"O you guardians of hell, indeed go to Puṣkarāvatī!
There, protect Mahākūṭa, who is surrounded by deities."
"Upon seeing him, you shall develop a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings.
Then those yakṣas, acting as Yama’s messengers, went to Puṣkarāvatī that very night;
they then saw [him] there, near the royal capital.
And that peaked structure was crowded with one door on every side.
The gods, nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras see the dead body with a *pratisarā* cord tied around its neck.
Surrounding him on all sides, they performed unsurpassed worship;
and those yakṣas established for him the name "Pratisarākūṭa."
Then those yakṣas, having returned once more, reported this decision of Yama, the King of Dharma, in detail:
"It is even so, O Lord, as you have stated.
Immediately upon the conclusion of those words, that great being cast off his body in the hells and was reborn among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
For that reason, he is called the Devaputra Pratisarāpūrvin.

Therefore, O Great Brāhmaṇa, because she has previously understood this, this Mahāpratisarā should be upheld, recited, and written; having placed it upon one's person according to the prescribed rite, it should be constantly worn.
He is constantly liberated from all calamities and sufferings; he crosses over all fears and terrors of the miserable destinies;
and it is not possible for lightning to strike him down.
Why was it recognized by Vidyut?

Formerly, Mahābrāhmaṇa, in the great city of Hiṅgumardana, there was a merchant named Vimalaśaṅkha, who was immensely wealthy with vast riches and gold, and possessed a treasury and storehouse filled to overflowing.
He was renowned as a great caravan leader (*mahāsārthavāha*).
Then, that great caravan leader, having obtained a ship, set out upon the great ocean.
(Mp_16) As far as the *timiṅgila* fish were concerned, that ship was held fast; and the *nāgas*, desiring to destroy it, became agitated and let out great roars and explosions.
They discharged lightning-torches and began to rain down thunderbolts.
Then those merchants, their minds struck by great suffering, [beheld] that great agitation of the *nāgas* and the lightning-torches.
They also unleashed thunderbolts; seeing the ship obstructed by those *timiṅgila* fish, he began to raise a great cry of lamentation.
They did not heed his specific entreaties.
Then, approaching the caravan leader, they spoke these piteous words:
"Save us, O Great Being; deliver us from this great terror!
Thereupon, the Great Caravan Leader, firm-minded and of great intelligence, spoke these words to the merchants who were overcome with despondency:
"Do not fear, do not fear! O merchants, display your heroism!
I shall deliver you from this great ocean of suffering.
Then, their minds filled with courage, the merchants spoke these words:

"O Great Being, tell us quickly and without delay: what is this? O High-minded One, as long as we live, let the greatness of your wisdom be told through your power; what will you do afterwards? Thereupon, the caravan leader recited this vidyā for them:
I possess a great vidyā, renowned by the name Pratisarā.
She is the crusher of all Buddhas, possessing great strength and prowess;
therefore, I shall liberate [you] from this great ocean of suffering.

Then, at that time, the great caravan leader, having written down this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells, caused it to be hoisted at the top of a banner. Immediately upon its being hoisted at the top of the banner, all those *timiṅgila* fish saw that ship become a single mass of flame.
Thereupon, those *nāgas*, with minds full of loving-kindness, descended before them and began to perform worship.
And those *timiṅgila* fish, being scorched by the power of this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells (*mahāvidyārājñī*),
fled away and departed wailing;
meanwhile, the merchants were brought by those great elephants to a vast island of great jewels.
This Great Knowledge, the Mahāpratisarā, is empowered by all the Tathāgatas; for that reason, O Great Brāhmaṇa, it is known as the "Great Knowledge.
Therefore, this must certainly be held, having been placed at the top of a banner.
It pacifies all winds, cold, untimely clouds, lightning, and thunderbolts;
it liberates one from all conflicts and disputes among gods, humans, and non-humans;
and [it protects against] all species of biting insects, mosquitoes, śarabhas, and various forms of living creatures.
Those who destroy the crops will have no power;
they shall be pacified.
All those with malicious minds—beasts, birds, and fanged creatures—shall perish.
And all flowers, fruits, leaves, trees, medicinal herbs, crops, and so forth will flourish;
they will become flavorful, delicious, and soft,
and they will be perfectly ripened.
The faults of excessive rain and drought will not exist at all;
there will be rain in due season, and never out of season.
And those great nāgas in that realm will release their showers of rain correctly, from time to time.
In whatever region this Queen of Vidyās named Mahāpratisarā shall circulate,
there those beings, having recognized it and having performed worship and honor, having surrounded it with various perfumes, various flowers, and various garments,
and having raised it upon the top of a banner over a shrine, [should do so] with various musical instruments and songs.
While playing musical instruments, they should circumambulate [the image];
then the deities, beginning with Śakra and Brahmā, will fulfill the hopes and aspirations of those Great Beings exactly as they have conceived them.
Alternatively, in whatever manner it is drawn according to the prescribed rite, in that very way it prospers:
one desiring a son obtains [one], another becomes pregnant, the fetus develops comfortably, and she gives birth with ease;
the fetus grows at the proper time and is released at the proper time.
Why is that, Great Brahmin? Listen as before.
In this very land of Magadha, there was a king named Prasāritapāṇi, and he was childless. Why was he known as Prasāritapāṇi?
Because as soon as he was born, he stretched out his hand, took hold of his mother’s breasts, and drank as much milk as he desired.
And those two breasts turned the color of gold by the mere touch [of his hand],
and they constantly increased with a great flow of milk;
for that reason, the name Prasāritapāṇi was established for that king.
Furthermore, whenever supplicants came to that king,
the king would extend his right hand into the air above; by that means, deities who were devoted to the Buddha would fill his hand with divine, exquisite jewels and gold gems.
Then that king bestowed gifts upon those beggars such that,
by mere thought, he granted all the desires for every kind of happiness and prosperity to all the beggars.
For the sake of obtaining a son, he performed great acts of worship and honor for the gods, yet he did not obtain a son.
He then began to perform worship and honor before the ancient stūpas of the Tathāgatas;
he offered great acts of worship and honor and gave gifts.
He observes the fast,
performs great and meritorious deeds,
and gives gifts that are truly inexhaustible.

For what reason? Great Brahmin, in the past, in this very realm of Magadha, in the city of Kuśinagara within the country called Malla— a preeminent great city— there lived under the teaching of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, a certain great being who had conceived the thought of Dharma, a merchant named Dharmamati.
Having established a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings, he taught the Dharma beginning with this very Great Knowledge, the Mahāpratisarā.
Then, a certain poor man, having heard that Dharma, spoke these words to the merchant:
"I shall perform labor as a hired servant in your noble house, and I shall listen to the Dharma."
"When I have something [to give], then I shall honor the Dharma.
While he was thus occupied with his household affairs and listening to the Dharma, at another time, a single dīnāra was given to him by the merchant.

Having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) for the sake of protecting all sentient beings and having made it common to all, he offered it as the Great Amulet Jewel (*Mahāpratisarāratna*).

Having made such a vow, he thought: "By this great fruit, may there be the cutting off of the suffering of poverty for myself and for all sentient beings. For this reason, that gift does not go to exhaustion.

Thus, having performed various and manifold accumulations of merit, and having worshipped the deities up to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the deities belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm then [appeared] in a dream.
He granted an audience and spoke thus:

"O Great King, this Great Dhāraṇī, the Queen of Great Mantras named Mahāpratisarā— the Aparājitā, the Heart of the Great Mudrā, the Wish-fulfilling Gem radiating with the purity of a garland of universal flames— is [to be bestowed] upon one who has observed the fast according to the ritual procedure as described."

"By binding [this] upon the body of the chief queen, you will then obtain a son. Then, at the end of that very night, the pure king assembled the family brahmins who were experts in calculation, writing, constellations, planets, and the fivefold analysis; and when the Puṣya constellation, the king of stars, had arrived, he had this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells, written according to the ritual prescribed in the manuals for the chief queen, whose limbs were well-washed and who had observed a fast, in accordance with the prescribed rite.
He tied it around his neck.
He performed great worship at the great stūpas of the Buddha and gave various excellent jewels as gifts to sentient beings.
Then, after nine months had passed, a son was born who was handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold.
He was endowed with the most excellent abundance of beautiful complexion.

Then, O Great Brāhmaṇa, having understood that she is the one who fulfills all desires, the invincible, renowned as the Great Amulet Jewel, the Queen of Great Vidyās worshipped by all the Tathāgatas— even for Śakra this is a crest-jewel. When Śakra, the lord of the gods, desired to engage in a great battle with the asuras, he then made this Great Vidyā his armor, entered the midst of the battle, placed it upon his crest, and having conquered all the asuras, lived in happiness.
He enters the city of the gods with well-being and security;
he shall become unassailable by all asuras.

For in this way, O Great Brahmin, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment onwards, for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who maintains this Great Amulet, the Great Queen of Vidyās, there is invincibility against all Māras.
It shall come to pass: whoever possesses this [mantra] in their throat will be empowered by all the Tathāgatas;
they will be protected by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
"He shall be constantly and perpetually saluted, honored, and revered by all gods, humans, non-humans, kings, royal ministers, brahmins, and householders;
he shall be worshipped and venerated by all gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
"He is a Great Being," he said.
The Blessed One, the crusher of Māra’s forces, shall be free from all diseases;
all his excessive calamities and misfortunes shall be pacified,
and for that Great Being, there shall be the disappearance of all sorrow.
All the deities will also constantly and perpetually provide him with protection, defense, and guardianship.

He should constantly and perpetually write down these four heart-essences of the *aparājita* great vidyā-mantra phrases, carry them on his body and around his neck, and maintain them; and he should also keep them constantly in mind.
When these are recited and meditated upon with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), all evil dreams, ill omens, and inauspicious states will perish,
and all forms of happiness and prosperity will manifest.
Herein, the mantra-words have been heard as perfected, performing every rite.
Namely: Oṃ amṛtavare vara vara pravara viśuddhe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ amṛtavilokini, protector of the womb, attractor, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
The Heart of Aparājitā.
Oṃ, O stainless one, O vast one, O victorious one, O excellent one, O immortal one, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

All the Buddhas without exception, together with the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, spoke these words of the dhāraṇī-mantra in a single unified voice, with a single resonant sound: "These heart-armor mantras of the Mahāpratisarā Great Vidyārājñī, these mantra-syllables, are sealed with the Dharma-seal of all the Tathāgatas."
Even hearing this is extremely rare for them, let alone writing, reciting, memorizing, reading, or explaining it to others; one should know that this is the work of a Buddha.
For this indeed utterly destroys all evil deeds;
it is praised, rejoiced in, and prophesied by all the Tathāgatas. This supreme, most rare great dhāraṇī named Aparājitā Mahāpratisarā—even the mere hearing of its name is extremely rare.
This [mantra] brings about the destruction of all evil;
it possesses great strength and prowess, great majesty, and great power; it manifests great virtues and shatters the hosts of deities belonging to the faction of Māra;
and it utterly eradicates all latent tendencies and their underlying connections.
It completely severs all the snares of Māra; it destroys those of evil intent who employ mantras, mudrās, poisons, *kākhorda* spells, magical rays, incantations, hostile rites, and sorcery.
It provides protection for those who take delight in being honored by the assembly of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble ones.
This is the protector of those devoted to the Mahāyāna through its upholding, writing, reciting, reading, chanting, hearing, and memorizing.
O Great Brāhmaṇa, this Mahāpratisarā, the Queen of Great Vidyās, is a great dhāraṇī that brings to fulfillment even the awakening of a Buddha;
she is not born anywhere [as an ordinary being], but everywhere receives great worship, just as I, the Teacher who has conquered all realms, do.
Why is it that she was previously fully known? (Mp_21)
O Mahābrahmā, this Great Queen of Vidyās is the destroyer of all obstacles and impediments.

And when the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipulaprahasitavadanamaṇikanakaratnajvalaraśmiprabhāsābhyudgatarāja, approached the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍala) and, having approached it, desired to turn the wheel of Dharma praised by all Buddhas, then all the Māras with their retinues— surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Māras— [approached].

Filled with various forms, misshapen figures, and terrifying, fearsome sounds, and empowered by the magical transformations of many diverse māras within their domains, they arrived manifesting showers of various weapons; having come, they surrounded him on all four sides and began to create obstacles.
Then the Blessed One, the King Exalted by the Radiant Splendor of Blazing Rays from Jewels, Gold, and Gems on His Face of Vast Laughter—
Having remained silent for a moment, he mentally recited this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells, seven times. Immediately upon its recitation, at that very instant,
all those wicked Māras saw from each and every pore of the Blessed One's body many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions [of deities].
Men clad in armor, with flaming swords, axes, nooses, mallets, scimitars, clubs, and tridents in their hands, proceed while uttering these words:
"Seize! Bind! Destroy the wicked Māras! Crush the evil-minded! Annihilate the life-force of all wicked grahas, obstacles, and vināyakas who seek to harm the Blessed One!"

Then, having utterly defeated all those wicked Māras with the sword of loving-kindness (*maitrī-khaḍga*), some were made to take up the precepts (*śikṣāpada*), while others were even prophesied (*vyākṛta*) for unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) there as beings of great power.

Furthermore, upon seeing those Great Beings (*mahāpuruṣa*) emerging from the pores of the Tathāgata’s skin, others in that city became distraught; deprived of their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), their eloquence, strength, and prowess destroyed, they were utterly ruined.
"All have fled in every direction. Then the Blessed One set in motion the Wheel of Dharma,
just as other Buddhas had done.
"Having utterly destroyed all obstacles, hindering spirits, and Māras, the Evil Ones, he has crossed over and reached the further shore.

Thus indeed, O Great Brahmā, this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Vidyās, having attained the perfection of great power, force, and psychic potency, liberates one from all calamities, fears, and terrors by the mere act of recollection.
It is for beings whose intentions are completely purified, and not for others who possess corrupt minds.
Therefore, O Great Brahmā, they should always be brought to mind through mere recollection;
and at all times, having written them down, they should be worn upon the body or kept around the neck.
Why is this? Listen as before.
In the great city of Ujjayinī, a certain man committed an offense against King Brahmadatta.
King Brahmadatta commanded his executioners:
"Go, deprive this man of his life."
Then those executioners, having seized that man ordered by the king, led him to a mountain cave; drawing their swords from their scabbards, they began to deprive that man of his life.
At that time, that man mentally recollected this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells (*mahāvidyārājñī*), and he wore it fastened upon his right arm.
By the power of this great spell of that Great Being, the sword burst into a single flame and shattered into pieces, scattered like dust.
Then those executioners reported this decision of theirs in detail to the king.
Thereupon the king, provoked and having become fierce, said:
"Go, sirs! In a certain region there is a yakṣa cave."
There dwell many hundreds of thousands of flesh-eating yakṣas; take him there and abandon him! Then that man was abandoned in that yakṣa cave by the executioners.
Immediately after it was cast into the yakṣa cave, all those yakṣas, with contented minds and joyful hearts, rushed forward, thinking, "We shall devour this human!

However, through the power of this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells, they saw that man as a single mass of flame, blazing intensely. Upon seeing his form, all those yakṣas were utterly terrified and perceived their own bodies as being on fire.
Then those yakṣas, overcome with amazement, seized that man, placed him outside the gate, and began to circumambulate him.
Meanwhile, those executioners reported this matter in detail to the king.
Thereupon, the king became even more enraged and, falling into a state of fury, said:
"Go, sirs, bind this man and throw him into the river!
Thereupon that man was bound by the executioners and thrown into the river. Immediately upon his being thrown in, that great man caused the river to become devoid of water, just as... (Mp_23)
The man remained standing right where he was on the ground,
and those bonds were shattered into pieces.
Having heard this, the king’s face blossomed with wonder, and he said:
"Aha! This wonder is seen in this man; what could be the cause of it? Such is my reflection. Then the king summoned that man and said to him:
"Do you know anything, O man?
That man replied,
"I do not know anything at all, Great King."
"Except for the Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Spells, whom I uphold;
this, O King, is its great power.
The king said:
Oh, what a great marvel!
This sublime Great Knowledge has been well-spoken;
it is the deluder of the rod of death and is empowered by all the Buddhas.
She is the savior of all sentient beings, the liberator from all suffering;
she is the great vidyā of great splendor, the deliverer from untimely death;
she was spoken by the compassionate Lords as the warder-off of great diseases.
Then, with a joyful mind, the king honored, revered, and rejoiced in the Mahāpratisarā, the Great Queen of Vidyās.
Having performed the ceremony of tying the cloth upon that man’s womb, he bestowed upon him the consecration for the position of chief of the city before his own people.
Thus indeed, O Great Brahmin, this Mahāpratisarā, the Great Queen of Vidyās, receives great honor everywhere.
It is unassailable by all those with wicked minds and is to be honored by all.
For in this way, O Great Brahmin, this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Vidyās, was never previously obstructed anywhere.
Therefore, this Queen of Great Vidyās must certainly be maintained, having been placed upon one's body or throat.
Moreover, Great Brahmin, this Queen of Great Spells should be written with a well-prepared field of cow dung and according to a most excellent ritual procedure.
Then that great brahmin, with a mind exceedingly joyful, prostrated before the Blessed One with the five-pointed salutation and began to ask:
"Venerable Blessed One, by what procedure should this Great Amulet, the Queen of Great Vidyās, be written?"
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, Great Brahmā; out of compassion for all sentient beings, I shall speak to you, so that beings may become happy and be liberated from the peril of karma."
It will serve for the liberation of those afflicted by disease, for the emergence of embryos in women,
and for the removal of the obstruction of poverty for sentient beings.
Having observed the fast on a lunar mansion considered auspicious for Puṣya,
one should be intent upon worshipping the Buddha and generate the mind set on awakening.
With a mind repeatedly imbued with compassion and endowed with loving-kindness,
he is constantly devoted to establishing the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having bathed with sandalwood, camphor, and musk-water,
and having put on clean garments perfumed with incense.
Then, having prepared a small altar smeared with cow dung, one should paint the auspicious mandala with powders of five colors.
And four full vases, with a fifth in the central mandala;
flowers, incense, and highly precious perfumes should be offered here.
Incense, sandalwood, spṛkkā, and likewise agallochum, along with the five sugars and gold, should be offered here according to the prescribed ritual.
Adorned with various kinds of flowers according to the season and according to the prescribed rite,
as well as all manner of flowers, fruits, seeds, and fragrances.
One should fill the offering jars with ghee, honey, milk, fire-wood, water, and so forth— those jars which are auspicious according to their characteristics.
One should place four [vessels] in the four directions and the fifth in the central mandala;
bowls filled with fragrance should also be placed in the corners.
Furthermore, four stakes made of khadira wood,
firmly fixed and driven in by the wise, having been bound with a five-colored thread,
should be placed in equal proportions outside the mandala, having first prostrated.
O Brahmin, having done this, one should draw [the diagram] if one desires success for oneself.
One who desires happiness should write [this] while consuming white food,
whether on a cloth, on birch bark, on paper, or wherever else it may be.
One who desires a son should indeed draw [the image] among women using genuine gorocana;
and in the center, one should depict a boy adorned with all ornaments.
Likewise, he should hold a bowl filled with jewels in his left hand,
seated upon a lotus that is fully blossomed and adorned.
One should cause a rain of jewels, necklaces, gold, and various kinds of precious gems to fall, and mountains should also be fashioned at the four corners.
One should thus write with diligence if one desires life and happiness;
a wise person should especially write it with saffron for men.
His desired undertakings will be accomplished; there is no doubt about this.
Various forms should be made, as well as the lotus-seal and its insignia.
One should draw two lotuses, or three, four, or five;
and likewise, one should fashion filaments for the lotuses on all sides.
One should fashion a well-flowered lotus together with its stalk and bound with a ribbon;
then, one should fashion a trident upon the lotus, with its corners likewise bound with ribbons.
One should fashion a battle-axe upon the lotus; then, on all sides of the petals, one should make a lotus together with a sword, and that lotus should indeed be sharp.
One should likewise fashion a conch upon the lotus; in all cases, one should perform the detailed ritual procedure.
A wise person should cause the ritual signs to be made everywhere.
One should avoid forms of children where the mind becomes corrupted;
however, forms of deities adorned with various ornaments should be fashioned.
One should depict a monk as Vajradhara for the purpose of threatening the wicked;
furthermore, one should draw the four Great Kings on the four sides.
One should depict Īśvara among Brāhmaṇas, Maheśvara among Kṣatriyas,
and one should always depict the gentle Cakrasvāmin among Śūdras.
Among the Vaiśyas, Vaiśravaṇa and Indra, the lord of the gods,
as well as the high-minded Prajāpati, should always be depicted for the sake of the boys.
If the woman is dark-complexioned, one should draw a fierce [deity] for her;
for a fair-complexioned woman, one should always draw a beautiful and illustrious one.
Maṇibhadra should be diligently depicted for the coarse [form], while Pūrṇabhadra is for the emaciated; this has indeed been declared by me, the Self-Existent One.
One should draw Mahākāla for a woman in her courses, and the deities of Brahmā;
one should also draw the others as previously described, according to what has been stated in detail.
Having written it down with diligence according to the prescribed ritual, one should constantly wear it around the neck; for him, there will be prosperity.
One should place a *cintāmaṇi* jewel at the front of the door; at the top of the banner, a lotus;
and upon the filaments of that lotus, a noose and likewise another wheel.
One should likewise draw a vajra upon a lotus, a mallet resting upon a lotus,
and a spear upon a lotus, as it is seen in the ritual injunctions.
All the jewels at the tops of the doorways should be filled with sparks,
and they should be bound with silk cloths according to the rules as proclaimed in the ritual manuals.
And the nāgas, bearing fruit, should be made with nine heads through the openings of jewels;
all of them should also be diligently established with a vajra in their hearts.
A wise person should always depict Sārthavāha as the power of kings;
for all the Vidyādharas, one should likewise depict Divyādevī.
One should draw the moon and sun, the lunar mansions, and the eight planets including Rāhu and Ketu; by drawing these fragments, the Pāṇḍavas will obtain a son.
Having written it down with certainty according to the prescribed rite and the ritual seen in the scriptures,
therefore a wise man should preserve it with every effort.
For this brings about all accomplishments, is auspicious, and destroys evil;
one attains the supreme state, according to the word of the Self-Existent One.
In this world there is supreme happiness, and in the next world there is supreme bliss;
his place shall be in the abode of the gods, beginning with the realm of the Thirty-three.
In the auspicious and delightful Jambudvīpa, the bliss of knowledge is eternal;
indeed, it cannot be fully described even by all the Buddhas, for it is a mass of merit.
Whatever merit a person who upholds the *Pratisarā* attains,
the gates to hell are closed and the gates to heaven are opened wide.
Endowed with great intelligence, he will attain happiness and prosperity;
and the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will constantly offer him encouragement.
Endowed with physical well-being and great strength,
he shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin), just as it was declared by the Conqueror Indra.
It will be a source of consolation for gods and kings, and a terror to those of evil mind;
this shall come to pass in time for him by whom this knowledge has been well-spoken.
He is not slain by weapon, nor by poison, nor by fire;
he suffers no untimely death, and evil deeds remain far from him.
Through seeing, touching, and even hearing it from all sides,
[one is freed from] quarrels with elemental spirits and demons, as well as fear of water and fire.
Wild beasts, predatory animals, serpents, and most terrible diseases—
all these shall not exist for those by whom this well-spoken vidyā has been mastered.
In every way, O all Māras, listen; I shall speak to you according to the truth:
they will become worthy of worship, for they are the supreme benefactors of all sentient beings.
The first chapter of the Noble Great Queen of Spells, the Mahāpratisarā, is completed.
Now, therefore, out of compassion for all sentient beings, I shall explain the ritual procedure for the protection of the possessor of knowledge (*vidyādhara*).
Through this ritual for the protection of people, great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*) will arise;
wherever protection is established, one becomes unbound—of this there is no doubt.
It is fearless and radiant, warding off all malevolent planets;
it is favorable to auspicious constellations and cuts through the accumulation of karmic bonds.
Whatever has been poorly consumed or transgressed, whatever has been done by all hosts of enemies,
whatever has been ill-beheld or ill-inscribed, and those terrible *kākhordas*— [may they be neutralized].
Poison prepared from powders and mantras, as well as ingested poison and *gara*—
all these are pacified for that person who causes this protection to be recited.
Those who transgress against this knowledge will be cooked by the Pratyaṅgirā;
so too will those fierce enemy armies and the great terrors of hostile foes.
They all fall into delirium, driven away by the *pratisarā* mantra;
the omniscient Buddhas and the foremost Bodhisattvas provide protection.
The Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas protect [them] from great fears,
as do many other various kinds of gods and Nāgas of great supernatural power.
These provide protection for that best of men who is constantly engaged with this Queen of Vidyās, merely by hearing it.
"He becomes fearless everywhere"—thus the Sage has declared;
[so too are overcome] bad dreams, evil deeds, and whatever calamities are terrible.
Those afflicted by diseases, those seized by great illnesses, those born of royal [karmic] retribution,
and others of many kinds of ailments, such as goiters, erysipelas, and scabies.
And those terrible calamities which devour the human race—
those most dreadful destroyers intended for the destruction of mankind.
All those powerful guardians flee as mere chatter wherever this [mantra] is employed;
however, one who has performed protection with this is released even when facing execution.
Even if one has been led to the abode of Yama by the noose of the time of death,
their lifespan shall increase through the mere writing of the Pratisarā.
But for one whose life-span is exhausted and who has already been dead for seven days, he will live merely by the act of writing this; of this there is no doubt.
Then, by merely hearing [this] according to the prescribed ritual, one obtains protection;
one attains well-being everywhere and lives happily according to one's desires.
Sixty-eight thousand, hundreds of millions,
and billions of Trāyastriṃśa gods, all with Śakra at their head.
And for the sake of protecting that being, the four world-protectors and the mighty Vajrapāṇi stood close behind him.
Together with hundreds of families of Vidyās, they constantly provide protection:
Soma, Sumatā, Sūrya, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Yama and Māṇibhadra, the mighty Baladeva,
the great hero Pūrṇabhadra, and Hārītī together with her children.
Pāñcāla and Pāñcika, Kārttikeya the lord of the Gaṇas, the Great Goddess Śrī, Vaiśravaṇa, and Sarasvatī.
Śaṅkhinī, Kūṭadantī, and likewise Ekajaṭā—
these fortunate and highly blessed ones provide constant protection.
I am the mother who gives birth to sons for the eunuchs and the one who nourishes the womb;
I shall be his great protector as long as he lives.
They always grant victory to men in battle, even in the terrifying conflict;
through this, the deities, certain of the Dharma, become bestowers of boons.
Furthermore, for the destruction of evil, it will succeed through the mere act of writing;
likewise, the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattvas will behold [the practitioner].
His fame shall increase, and his merit and lifespan shall increase;
there is no doubt that his wealth, grain, and prosperity will flourish.
The wise person sleeps in peace and awakens in peace;
they are invincible to all enemies and even to the hosts of all living beings.
For one engaged in battle, victory is constant;
while this spell is being mastered, it serves as an unsurpassed protection.
One shall accomplish the vidyā with ease, and no obstacle shall arise for him;
all ritual manuals shall be perfected once he has entered every maṇḍala.
And he shall quickly become a knower of the samaya in all births;
and by upholding the virtues [of the Buddhas], he shall become a trusted confidant of the Jinas.
Endowed with all auspiciousness, it fulfills every success and every desire;
as soon as this is written, all happiness flourishes.
Having passed away in happiness, one shall be destined for heaven,
even in the midst of disputes, quarrels, and most dreadful conflicts.
Completely liberated from all fears, just as the word of the Victor has spoken, they will always remember their past lives; of this there is no doubt.
Kings, the members of his harem, and the great multitude of people shall always be under his control, along with his ministers, who are virtuous and esteemed by the world.
They will be beloved by all, both gods and humans;
and they will constantly provide protection for them, day and night.

O Great Brahmin, for whomever protection, concealment, rescue, acceptance, preservation, peace, well-being, avoidance of punishment, avoidance of weapons, the neutralization of poison, and the destruction of poison have been performed by means of this form of the Tathāgata which holds the words of the vidyā-mantra;
His exhausted lifespan increases once again;
he lives happily for a very long time and becomes endowed with mindfulness.
By mere recitation or by the stroking with a vajra, one is liberated from untimely death and from great diseases;
all his illnesses are pacified,
and even long-standing ailments come to an end through mere stroking.
By practicing daily recitation, one becomes possessed of great wisdom;
one becomes endowed with vitality, strength, vigor, and eloquence;
and all his karmic obscurations that are destined to be experienced will go to complete exhaustion without remainder.
Furthermore, all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and others will infuse their vital essence, strength, and vigor into his body;
he will abound in great joy.

At the very least, O Great Brahmā, even for those born as animals—beasts or birds—who hear this protection of the mantra-words of the Great Vidyā fall upon the cavity of their ears, they shall all become irreversible from enlightenment.

Whether it be a kṣatriya, or someone else, whoever shall hear it, and having heard it, shall with great faith, reverence, and resolute intention write it down, cause it to be written, preserve it, recite it,
or cultivate it with an intense mind.
And he will proclaim it in detail to others;
for him, O Great Brahmans, the eight types of untimely death shall not prevail,
nor shall great diseases arise in his body.

Neither fire, nor poison, nor weapons, nor *gara* poison, nor *kākhorda* spells, nor [malevolent] rays, nor the practice of mantras, nor the application of powders, nor pain in the limbs, nor ailments affecting the head— neither the fever that recurs every day, every second day, every fourth day, nor the fever lasting a week— shall overcome him; mindful, he sleeps in peace and well-being.
Upon merely being remembered, one awakens;
one will attain the Great Parinirvāṇa,
and together with the Dharma, one simultaneously attains great sovereignty.
Wherever he is reborn, in each and every birth he will be one who remembers his former lives;
he will be dear to all sentient beings,
and he will be a person worthy of veneration.
He will be completely liberated from rebirth in all the realms of hell, the animal realm, and the host of hungry ghosts.
Just as the orb of the sun provides illumination with its rays for all sentient beings, so shall he become a maker of light through his radiance.
Just as the orb of the moon refreshes the bodies of all sentient beings with its flowing nectar, so shall he refresh the mental continuums of all sentient beings with the nectar of the Dharma.

All malevolent yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, those who cause insanity, epilepsy, and possession by ḍākinīs, as well as obstructing spirits and destroyers— none of these are able to cause harm through the power of this Great Amulet,
the Great Vidyā. And when they approach, this Queen of Vidyās should be recollected.
Then all those evil-minded ones will become subject to the Vidyādhara and obedient to his command upon hearing it.
By the power of this very Great Amulet, the Great Queen of Vidyās, he shall have no fear of enemies,
and he shall be one who cannot be overcome.
By all hosts of enemies— including kings, great kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders—
and even by executioners, though he may be deserving of death, the raised weapons shall break into pieces, crumbling like dust; and then, at that time, all dharmas will become manifest before him.
And his power of mindfulness will become great;
for this is a supreme destroyer of demons, a purifier that destroys evil,
and it brings prosperity, bestows wisdom, and increases all virtuous qualities.
For she brings all auspiciousness to them and destroys all inauspiciousness;
she causes the seeing of good dreams and destroys bad dreams.
For this is a powerful protective vidyā for both women and men;
in forests, wildernesses, and difficult terrains, they are always liberated from danger at that very moment.
And one obtains all desires, just as stated in the Buddha’s word.
If they have entered upon a wrong path, one should recollect this knowledge for them.
One quickly finds the path, as well as excellent food and drink,
[the results of] whatever was done through action, mind, or speech in previous births.
Whatever various kinds of impurity there may be, it will all be destroyed through recollection, retention, grasping, and even by writing.
Through reciting, speaking, mastering, and teaching it to others,
he will before long have attained the realization of the nature of all phenomena.
For when the essence of the Dharma is thus attained, the wicked go to their destruction;
all actions are accomplished, whatever is desired by the mind.
And in the face of all fear of death, he shall be their protection—
whether from kings, fire, water, lightning, or even thieves.
Battles, conflicts, quarrels, and those who are fierce fanged creatures—
all these vanish into mere chatter once one hundred thousand recitations of this vidyā have been completed.
One should know this supreme, perfected vidyā, taught indeed by all the Buddhas;
those possessed of renown do not falter in fulfilling the accumulations for enlightenment.
And in all circumstances whatsoever, one should employ this vidyā for whatever tasks one desires for the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others.
They are accomplished effortlessly through this vidyā; there is no doubt about this.
Homage to all the Tathāgatas who abide in the ten directions!

Oṃ maṇivajre, O you who are hostile to the heart, O you who rend the army of Māra! Strike, strike all enemies! Protect, protect my body and that of all sentient beings! Vajre, vajre; Vajragarbhe, vajragarbhe! Terrify, terrify all the abodes of Māra! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
Buddha-maitrī, empowered by the vajra-aeon of all Tathāgatas, remove all karmic obscurations! Svāhā!
Now I shall explain the medical treatment for the sick:
one should prepare a square mandala mixed with clay and cow dung.
The wise one should decorate the auspicious mandala with five-colored powders and,
according to the ritual procedure, place four full vases there.
One should scatter flowers there, burn the finest incense,
and perform the bali-offering ritual for the *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī*.
As before, one should offer incense, flowers, and so forth here according to the ritual rules;
four square mats should be placed there, all of them bound with silk cloths.
Having first attended to the patient, one should subsequently have him enter the central maṇḍala, clothed in clean garments with his limbs anointed with auspicious fragrances.
Sitting facing the east, one should recite this knowledge;
the wise person should provide protection for him by reciting it seven times.
Then, for the sake of the sick person, one should recite this vidyā twenty-one times for the pacification of all diseases.
Furthermore, having consecrated the water-pot seven times with the mantra,
the practitioner should subsequently pour the water and flowers according to the prescribed rite.
In this manner, one should cast exactly seven [offerings] on the right side;
likewise, let there be exactly seven in the western direction and in the northern direction as well.
Furthermore, seven protections shall be established both below and above;
when this is done, O best of the twice-born, one is liberated from all suffering.
This protection has been proclaimed by me; it was spoken by the Lion of the Śākyas.
There is no other protection or vidyā superior to this in the three realms.

For one whose mental continuum has cultivated wisdom, there is neither death, nor old age, nor disease, nor ever the state of separation from those dear; nor indeed is there union with those unpleasant. For even Yama, the excellent King of Dharma, will pay him honor with reverence.
Indeed, it shall be told that you must go to the battle between the gods and the asuras; for a moment, you will cause this city of hell to blaze.
Then, by means of celestial palaces of many kinds, you, possessing great supernatural power, will go to the auspicious abode of the gods.
Thus, he shall always be honored there by humans, gods, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
Vajrapāṇi, the lord of yakṣas, and Indra, the husband of Śacī; Hārītī and Pāñcika, as well as the world-protectors of great supernatural power.
The moon and the sun together with the constellations, those planets that are most terrible,
as well as all the great nāgas, deities, and ṛṣis;
Asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas—
whose great power of spells is for the sake of constant, awakened protection— [are present].
The wise one, possessing great supernatural power, should wear this written [text] bound upon his arm;
he shall constantly obtain great honor and prosperity as well.
The ritual procedure for the protection of the Vidyādhara belonging to the Great Amulet, the King of Vidyās, is completed.
